cards.q: Which arrangement of processes defines a multipolar neuron?
cards.a: Many dendrites and one axon leaving the cell body.
options: Two processes, one dendrite and one axon, at opposite ends
One process that leaves the cell body and then splits in two
Many dendrites and a single axon leaving the cell body
Many axons and a single dendrite leaving the cell body
cards.explanation: Multipolar means many poles: numerous dendrites plus one axon, so the cell can gather input from thousands of synapses and send one output. A single process that branches in two is the pseudounipolar pattern of sensory ganglion cells. Two processes at opposite ends describe a bipolar neuron. No neuron carries many axons, because each cell has a single trigger zone and one all-or-none output line.

cards.q: Which structural class has exactly two processes, one dendrite and one axon, extending from opposite ends of the cell body?
cards.a: Bipolar.
options: Bipolar
Pseudounipolar
Multipolar
Anaxonic
cards.explanation: A bipolar neuron has one receptive process and one axon leaving from opposite poles, an arrangement that suits a cell relaying a signal straight through. Multipolar cells have many dendrites and one axon. Pseudounipolar cells have a single stalk that splits into peripheral and central branches. Anaxonic neurons have no process identifiable as an axon and are found in small numbers in the retina and brain.

cards.q: In a pseudounipolar neuron, where does the cell body sit relative to the conducting pathway?
cards.a: Off to one side, so the signal does not pass through it.
options: At the receptive end, where the stimulus is transduced
In line with the axon, midway along the conducting path
Inside the spinal cord, at the central end of the fiber
Off to one side of a single process the signal runs along
cards.explanation: The single stalk splits into a peripheral branch and a central branch, and the cell body hangs off that stalk, so the action potential travels straight past it. Putting the cell body at the receptive end describes a bipolar sensory cell such as an olfactory neuron. Placing it in line with the axon would force every signal through the soma and slow conduction. The cell body of these neurons lies in a ganglion outside the cord, not inside it.

cards.q: A neuron whose axon carries signals from a skin receptor toward the spinal cord is called what?
cards.a: An afferent neuron.
options: An afferent neuron
An efferent neuron
An interneuron
A preganglionic neuron
cards.explanation: Afferent means carried toward the central nervous system, which is exactly what a sensory fiber does. Efferent is the opposite direction, out from the CNS to muscle or gland. An interneuron lies entirely inside the CNS and connects other neurons rather than reaching a receptor. A preganglionic neuron is a specific kind of efferent cell in the autonomic system, so it also points away from the CNS.

cards.q: Which functional class accounts for the great majority of neurons in the human nervous system?
cards.a: Interneurons.
options: Sensory neurons
Motor neurons
Preganglionic autonomic neurons
Interneurons
cards.explanation: Interneurons vastly outnumber the other classes because almost all of the brain and spinal cord is devoted to processing between input and output. Sensory neurons are numerous but are limited to the afferent pathways. Motor neurons are the smallest group, since many inputs converge onto each one before it drives a muscle. Preganglionic autonomic cells are a small subset of the motor side.

cards.q: Where are the cell bodies of the pseudounipolar neurons that carry skin sensation located?
cards.a: In the dorsal root ganglion, outside the spinal cord.
options: In the dorsal horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the dorsal root ganglion, outside the spinal cord
In the ventral horn of the spinal cord gray matter
In the skin itself, next to the sensory ending
cards.explanation: These first-order sensory cell bodies cluster in the dorsal root ganglion, a swelling on the dorsal root just outside the cord. The dorsal horn holds the second-order neurons these fibers synapse on, not the sensory cell bodies themselves. The ventral horn holds somatic motor neurons. The peripheral ending in the skin is only the receptive terminal; the nucleus and protein synthesis stay in the ganglion.

cards.q: Bipolar neurons are found in which locations in the human body?
cards.a: The retina and the olfactory epithelium.
options: The dorsal root ganglia and the autonomic ganglia
The ventral horn and the cerebral cortex
The retina and the olfactory epithelium
The cerebellum and the hippocampus
cards.explanation: Bipolar cells serve special senses where a signal is passed straight along a short chain, notably the retina and the olfactory epithelium, with a similar pattern in the inner ear. Dorsal root ganglia hold pseudounipolar cells, and autonomic ganglia hold multipolar ones. The ventral horn, cortex, cerebellum and hippocampus are all populated by multipolar neurons that integrate many inputs.

cards.q: A somatic motor neuron in the ventral horn belongs to which structural class?
cards.a: Multipolar.
options: Bipolar
Multipolar
Pseudounipolar
Anaxonic
cards.explanation: A motor neuron must sum input from descending tracts, afferent fibers and local interneurons before it fires, and the multipolar shape with many dendrites provides that receptive surface. Bipolar cells relay a single line of information and are limited to special sensory epithelia. Pseudounipolar cells are sensory, with cell bodies in ganglia. An anaxonic cell has no axon and so could not drive a muscle a meter away.

cards.q: A retinal neuron has one short process ending on photoreceptors and a single axon leaving the opposite side of the cell body. Which structural class is it?
cards.a: Bipolar.
options: Multipolar
Bipolar
Pseudounipolar
Anaxonic
cards.explanation: Two processes leaving opposite poles is the definition of bipolar, and the retina is one of the few places this class appears. Multipolar would require many dendrites converging on the soma. Pseudounipolar would show a single stalk splitting into two branches with the soma set off to the side. An anaxonic cell would have no identifiable axon at all, so the described axon rules it out.

cards.q: A neuron has its cell body in a dorsal root ganglion, a peripheral branch ending in a muscle spindle, and a central branch entering the spinal cord. Which structural class is it?
cards.a: Pseudounipolar.
options: Pseudounipolar
Multipolar
Anaxonic
Bipolar
cards.explanation: One stalk that divides into a peripheral and a central branch, with the soma parked in a ganglion off to the side, is the pseudounipolar plan used by essentially all first-order somatic sensory neurons. Bipolar cells have their soma between the two processes rather than off to the side. Multipolar cells have many dendrites and are the integrating cells of the CNS. Anaxonic cells lack an axon and cannot project a meter to the cord.

cards.q: A neuron lies entirely within the spinal cord gray matter, receiving input from an incoming sensory fiber and synapsing on a motor neuron. Which functional class is it?
cards.a: An interneuron.
options: An afferent neuron
An efferent neuron
An interneuron
A postganglionic neuron
cards.explanation: A cell that begins and ends inside the central nervous system, bridging input to output, is by definition an interneuron. An afferent neuron would have to reach a receptor in the periphery. An efferent neuron would have to send its axon out of the CNS to a muscle or gland. A postganglionic autonomic neuron sits in a peripheral ganglion, outside the cord entirely.

cards.q: An axon leaves the brainstem and ends on a salivary gland. Which functional class does this neuron belong to?
cards.a: Efferent.
options: Efferent
Afferent
Interneuron
Second-order sensory
cards.explanation: The axon carries the signal away from the CNS to an effector, and a gland is an effector just as a muscle is, so the cell is efferent. Afferent would require the signal to travel toward the CNS from a receptor. An interneuron never leaves the CNS. A second-order sensory neuron carries sensation upward inside the CNS and does not innervate glands.

cards.q: Why does the multipolar shape suit a neuron that must combine input from thousands of other neurons?
cards.a: Its many dendrites provide a large receptive surface for synapses.
options: Its single stalk lets signals bypass the cell body entirely
Its two processes keep the input and output paths separate
Its short axon prevents any loss of signal between cells
Its many dendrites give a large surface for synaptic input
cards.explanation: Dendritic branching multiplies membrane area, and each patch of that area can host synapses whose graded potentials then sum at the trigger zone. Bypassing the soma through a single stalk is the pseudounipolar arrangement, which favors speed rather than integration. Separating input from output along two processes describes a bipolar relay cell. Multipolar axons are often long, and axon length is not what makes the cell a good integrator.

cards.q: In a pseudounipolar sensory neuron, what happens to an action potential travelling from the skin toward the spinal cord when it reaches the level of the cell body?
cards.a: It stays on the shared stalk and bypasses the cell body.
options: It stops, and a new potential is started in the central branch
It is amplified by the cell body before it continues centrally
It stays on the shared stalk and bypasses the cell body
It reverses direction and travels back toward the receptor
cards.explanation: The soma sits on a side stalk, so the impulse runs continuously from the peripheral branch into the central branch without a synapse or a detour, which keeps conduction fast. Nothing stops and restarts, because there is no synapse within a single neuron. The cell body does not amplify impulses; action potential size is set by the axon membrane. Backward travel is prevented by the refractory period behind the impulse.

cards.q: A peripheral ganglion is examined and every neuron in it has a single process leaving a round cell body wrapped by satellite cells. Which functional class are these neurons?
cards.a: Afferent neurons carrying sensation to the CNS.
options: Somatic efferent neurons supplying skeletal muscle
Afferent neurons carrying sensation to the CNS
Interneurons of the spinal cord gray matter
Postganglionic sympathetic neurons supplying blood vessels
cards.explanation: A single process is the pseudounipolar giveaway, and pseudounipolar cell bodies in peripheral ganglia are sensory, so this is a dorsal root or cranial sensory ganglion. Somatic motor cell bodies never sit in peripheral ganglia; they stay in the ventral horn or brainstem. Interneurons are confined to the CNS. Postganglionic sympathetic neurons do live in peripheral ganglia, but they are multipolar and would show several dendrites.

cards.q: A single spinal dorsal root is cut. Predict the effect in the region that root serves and name the class of neuron lost.
cards.a: Sensation is lost and movement is preserved, because pseudounipolar afferents were cut.
options: Movement is lost, sensation is spared, multipolar efferents cut
Sensation is lost, movement is spared, pseudounipolar afferents cut
Both are lost, because the root carries afferent and efferent fibers
Neither is lost, because interneurons reroute around the cut root
cards.explanation: The dorsal root carries only the central branches of pseudounipolar sensory neurons, so cutting it removes input while leaving the ventral root motor output intact. Lost movement with spared sensation describes a ventral root lesion instead. Afferent and efferent fibers do travel together, but only after the two roots join to form the spinal nerve, so at the root itself they are separable. Interneurons cannot substitute for information that never reaches the cord.

cards.q: After an injury, a muscle is paralyzed but skin sensation over that muscle is normal. Which neurons were damaged and where do their cell bodies lie?
cards.a: Multipolar efferents with cell bodies in the ventral horn.
options: Pseudounipolar afferents with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
Bipolar relay neurons with cell bodies inside the dorsal horn
Multipolar efferents with cell bodies in the ventral horn
Interneurons with cell bodies in the dorsal root ganglion
cards.explanation: Preserved sensation with lost movement isolates the lesion to the efferent limb, and somatic motor neurons are multipolar cells whose somata sit in the ventral horn. Damaging pseudounipolar afferents would have produced the opposite pattern, numbness with intact strength. Bipolar neurons are not found in the spinal cord at all. Interneurons live in the CNS, not in a peripheral ganglion, so that pairing is impossible.

cards.q: A disease destroys the bipolar neurons of the retina while photoreceptors and ganglion cells survive. What is the predicted result?
cards.a: Light is still transduced but the signal cannot reach the ganglion cells.
options: Light is still transduced but the signal cannot reach the ganglion cells
Ganglion cells fire continuously once their normal inhibition is removed
Vision is unaffected, since photoreceptors contact ganglion cells directly
Light is no longer transduced, so no receptor potential is generated
cards.explanation: Bipolar cells are the relay in the retinal chain from photoreceptor to ganglion cell, so losing them breaks the path even though transduction and the output neurons are intact. Photoreceptors do not synapse directly on ganglion cells, which is why the bipolar layer matters. Loss of a relay removes drive rather than removing inhibition, so continuous firing is not expected. Transduction happens in the photoreceptor outer segment and is untouched here.

cards.q: A toxin destroys most interneurons in the spinal cord gray matter but spares afferent and efferent neurons. Which response is most impaired?
cards.a: Polysynaptic withdrawal reflexes.
options: Transduction at the sensory receptor in the skin
Transmission at the neuromuscular junction
The monosynaptic stretch reflex, such as the knee jerk
Polysynaptic withdrawal reflexes from a painful stimulus
cards.explanation: A withdrawal reflex routes the afferent signal through one or more interneurons before reaching motor neurons, so removing interneurons breaks the circuit. Receptor transduction is a property of the afferent ending and needs no interneuron. Neuromuscular transmission happens between a motor neuron and muscle, well outside the cord. The stretch reflex is the useful contrast: its afferent synapses directly on the motor neuron, so it survives when interneurons are lost.

cards.q: Which type of electrical signal do the dendrites of a neuron carry?
cards.a: Graded potentials.
options: Graded potentials that vary in size with the input
All-or-none action potentials of fixed amplitude
End plate potentials generated by acetylcholine
Pacemaker potentials that depolarize on a set schedule
cards.explanation: Dendritic membrane responds to transmitter with graded potentials whose amplitude tracks how much transmitter bound and which fade as they spread toward the soma. Action potentials are all-or-none and begin only at the trigger zone, where voltage-gated Na+ channels are dense. End plate potentials are the graded response of skeletal muscle at the neuromuscular junction, not of a dendrite. Pacemaker potentials belong to cardiac nodal and some smooth muscle cells.

cards.q: Which region of a neuron is the trigger zone, where action potentials are initiated?
cards.a: The axon hillock and initial segment of the axon.
options: The tips of the dendrites, where transmitter first binds
The axon hillock and the initial segment of the axon
The center of the cell body, next to the nucleus
The axon terminal, just before transmitter is released
cards.explanation: The trigger zone is the cone-shaped hillock plus the first stretch of axon, the place where summed graded potentials are read against threshold. Dendritic tips receive input but lack the channel density to fire. The soma conducts graded signals toward the hillock but does not initiate them. The terminal is the output end, and by the time the impulse arrives there the decision to fire has already been made.

cards.q: Which membrane property of the trigger zone explains why the action potential starts there rather than on a dendrite?
cards.a: It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels.
options: It has the thinnest membrane in the whole neuron
It has the largest surface area of any neuronal region
It has the highest density of voltage-gated Na+ channels
It has the greatest number of Na+/K+ ATPase pumps
cards.explanation: Packing voltage-gated Na+ channels into the hillock and initial segment lowers the threshold there, so that region reaches firing level before any other part of the cell. Membrane thickness is essentially uniform across a cell and is not what sets excitability. Dendrites, not the hillock, carry the largest surface area, which is why they receive input rather than initiate output. Na+/K+ ATPase maintains the gradients over minutes and hours but does not generate the upstroke of an action potential.

cards.q: What kind of signal travels along the axon?
cards.a: Action potentials of constant amplitude.
options: Graded potentials that shrink as they travel
Receptor potentials proportional to stimulus strength
Action potentials of constant, all-or-none amplitude
Slow waves that set a rhythm for firing
cards.explanation: Once threshold is crossed the axon regenerates the same size impulse at every point along its length, which is what lets a signal reach a target a meter away without fading. Graded potentials do shrink with distance, which is exactly why they cannot serve as the long-distance signal. Receptor potentials are graded events at sensory endings. Slow waves are a smooth muscle phenomenon, not a feature of axons.

cards.q: What is the immediate result of an action potential arriving at the axon terminal?
cards.a: Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ enters the terminal.
options: Transmitter is synthesized from precursors delivered by the soma
The Na+/K+ ATPase reverses and pumps Na+ back inward
Voltage-gated Ca2+ channels open and Ca2+ enters the terminal
The terminal membrane becomes permanently depolarized
cards.explanation: Depolarization of the terminal opens voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, and the Ca2+ that rushes in is the signal that makes vesicles fuse and release transmitter. The Na+/K+ ATPase never reverses under physiological conditions; it restores gradients in one direction only. Transmitter synthesis happens over minutes to hours and is not the immediate event triggered by one impulse. The terminal repolarizes within milliseconds, so permanent depolarization would mean the cell had failed.

cards.q: Which function belongs to the cell body of a neuron?
cards.a: Synthesizing the proteins the rest of the cell needs.
options: Synthesizing the proteins that the rest of the neuron needs
Releasing neurotransmitter onto the next cell in the circuit
Initiating the action potential once threshold is reached
Regenerating the impulse at each node along the axon
cards.explanation: The soma holds the nucleus and the rough endoplasmic reticulum seen as Nissl substance, so it makes the channels, enzymes and cytoskeletal proteins that keep a long axon working. Initiating the impulse is the job of the trigger zone just downstream. Transmitter release happens at the terminal. Regeneration of the impulse at nodes is an axonal event and does not involve the cell body at all.

cards.q: What is the axon hillock?
cards.a: The cone-shaped part of the cell body where the axon begins.
options: The swelling at the end of the axon that stores vesicles
The gap in the myelin sheath along the length of the axon
The branching region where dendrites leave the cell body
The cone-shaped part of the cell body where the axon begins
cards.explanation: The hillock is the tapering region of the soma from which the axon emerges, and together with the initial segment it forms the trigger zone. The swelling at the far end is the axon terminal, the release site. Dendrites arise from the soma too, but that region has no special name and no concentration of voltage-gated channels. A gap in myelin is a node of Ranvier, which lies far downstream along the axon.

cards.q: Which statement describes a graded potential?
cards.a: Its amplitude varies with stimulus strength and it decays with distance.
options: Its size varies with the stimulus and it decays with distance
It travels the length of the axon without losing amplitude
It cannot be summed with other potentials in the same cell
It is the same size no matter how strong the stimulus is
cards.explanation: Graded means the response scales with the input, and because current leaks across the membrane as it spreads, the signal is smaller the farther it travels from where it started. A fixed size regardless of stimulus describes the all-or-none action potential. Travelling without decrement is also an action potential property, achieved by regenerating the signal. Summation is precisely what graded potentials are for, since it is how the trigger zone adds up its inputs.

cards.q: Two identical excitatory synapses fire, one on a distal dendrite and one on the cell body near the hillock. Which produces the larger depolarization at the trigger zone?
cards.a: The synapse on the cell body, because its graded potential decays less.
options: The dendritic synapse, because dendrites amplify their own input
The synapse on the cell body, because its signal decays less
Both equally, because graded potentials do not lose amplitude
Neither, because only the axon can carry signals to the hillock
cards.explanation: A graded potential loses amplitude as it spreads, so the input starting closest to the trigger zone arrives with more of its depolarization intact. Dendrites do not amplify; they receive and conduct passively in most neurons. Loss of amplitude with distance is the defining weakness of graded potentials, so equality is not expected. The soma and dendrites conduct these local currents perfectly well toward the hillock, which is how integration happens at all.

cards.q: A sensory stimulus is doubled in strength. What happens to the action potentials the neuron sends down its axon?
cards.a: They stay the same size but occur more frequently.
options: They become twice as large but keep the same frequency
They become both larger and more frequent
They stay the same size but occur more frequently
They stop, because the axon is overloaded by the input
cards.explanation: The all-or-none rule fixes action potential amplitude, so intensity has to be coded some other way, and the nervous system uses firing frequency. Doubling the amplitude would violate the all-or-none property of the axon membrane. Since amplitude cannot change, the combined option fails for the same reason. Very strong input increases firing rate up to a limit set by the refractory period, but it does not silence the axon.

cards.q: A drug blocks the voltage-gated Ca2+ channels in the axon terminal only. Predict what happens when an action potential reaches that terminal.
cards.a: The impulse arrives normally but no transmitter is released.
options: The impulse fails partway along the axon before reaching the terminal
The impulse arrives normally but no transmitter is released
The trigger zone can no longer reach threshold and stops firing
Transmitter is released continuously instead of in response to firing
cards.explanation: Conduction along the axon depends on voltage-gated Na+ and K+ channels, so the impulse still arrives; what is lost is the Ca2+ entry that couples arrival to vesicle fusion. Conduction failure would require blocking axonal Na+ channels rather than terminal Ca2+ channels. The trigger zone lies far upstream of the drug and is unaffected. Blocking Ca2+ entry removes the release signal rather than making release continuous.

cards.q: An action potential is recorded at the trigger zone and again halfway down an unbranched axon. How do the two amplitudes compare?
cards.a: They are the same, because the impulse is regenerated as it travels.
options: The two are the same, because the impulse is regenerated as it travels
The midpoint signal is larger, because the axon narrows along its length
The midpoint signal is about half as large, because current leaks out
The midpoint signal is smaller only if the stimulus was weak
cards.explanation: Each patch of axon membrane opens its own voltage-gated Na+ channels and rebuilds the impulse at full size, so amplitude is preserved from hillock to terminal. Decay with distance is a property of graded potentials, which do not regenerate. Axon diameter affects conduction speed rather than impulse height, and a narrowing axon would not raise amplitude. Stimulus strength sets firing frequency, not the size of any single action potential.

cards.q: Two excitatory synapses on different dendrites of the same neuron are active at the same instant, and together they bring the trigger zone to threshold. What is this called?
cards.a: Spatial summation.
options: Temporal summation
Saltatory conduction
Accommodation
Spatial summation
cards.explanation: Inputs arriving at the same moment from different places on the cell add together at the trigger zone, which is spatial summation. Temporal summation is the other route to threshold, where one input repeats quickly enough that each graded potential builds on the last. Saltatory conduction describes impulses jumping between nodes along a myelinated axon, a different process entirely. Accommodation is the loss of excitability during a slow depolarization.

cards.q: An inhibitory synapse on the cell body produces a hyperpolarizing graded potential just as an excitatory input arrives. What is the effect at the trigger zone?
cards.a: The two sum, so the membrane is less likely to reach threshold.
options: The excitatory input is blocked from reaching the trigger zone
The inhibitory signal cancels the action potential after it starts
The two sum, so the membrane is less likely to reach threshold
The threshold voltage itself is shifted to a more negative value
cards.explanation: Graded potentials add algebraically, so a hyperpolarizing input subtracts from a depolarizing one and the net voltage at the trigger zone falls short of threshold more easily. An action potential, once started, runs to completion and cannot be cancelled midway. The excitatory potential is not blocked; it still spreads to the hillock and simply meets opposition. Threshold is a property of the channels at the trigger zone and does not move because of a synaptic input.

cards.q: You want to record a signal whose amplitude changes when you change how much transmitter is applied. Which region should you place the electrode in?
cards.a: A dendrite or the cell body.
options: The middle of the axon
A dendrite or the cell body
The initial segment, just past the hillock
A node of Ranvier along the axon
cards.explanation: Only the graded signals of the dendrites and soma scale with input size, so that is where a dose-dependent amplitude shows up. The axon carries all-or-none impulses whose amplitude is fixed no matter how strong the input was. A node of Ranvier is simply a point on the axon and follows the same all-or-none rule. The initial segment is where the graded signal is converted into a fixed-size impulse, so recordings there already show the all-or-none output.

cards.q: A neuron rests at -70 mV and fires at -55 mV. One excitatory input starts as a 15 mV depolarization at a dendrite but has decayed to 5 mV by the time it reaches the trigger zone. How many such inputs must arrive together to fire the cell?
cards.a: Three.
options: Two
Five
One, because the dendritic value is what counts
Three
cards.explanation: The cell needs 15 mV of depolarization at the trigger zone to move from -70 to -55, and each input delivers 5 mV there, so three simultaneous inputs are required. Two would give only 10 mV and leave the membrane at -60 mV, still below threshold. Using the 15 mV starting value ignores the decay that happens on the way, which is the whole point of the calculation. Five would be more than needed, since 15 mV is reached at three.

cards.q: A local anesthetic is applied to a narrow band in the middle of an axon, blocking voltage-gated Na+ channels there only. Predict the recordings at the trigger zone and at the axon terminal.
cards.a: Normal impulses at the trigger zone, none at the terminal.
options: No impulse at either site, because the whole neuron is silenced
Normal impulses at the trigger zone but none at the terminal
Normal impulses at both sites, since the block affects only speed
Impulses at the terminal only, arriving from the opposite direction
cards.explanation: Synaptic input and threshold detection happen upstream of the drug, so the trigger zone fires normally, but the impulse cannot regenerate through the blocked band and dies there, leaving the terminal silent. The neuron is not silenced everywhere, because the anesthetic reaches only the treated band. Blocking Na+ channels prevents regeneration outright rather than slowing it. Nothing generates impulses distal to the block, so the terminal has no other source.

cards.q: A neuron is altered so that the threshold at its trigger zone moves from -55 mV to -45 mV, with the resting potential unchanged at -70 mV. What is the predicted effect on the cell?
cards.a: It needs more summed input to fire, so it fires less readily.
options: It needs more summed input to fire, so it fires less readily
It fires at the same rate, since threshold does not affect firing
It fires continuously, since the resting potential now exceeds threshold
It fires more readily, since threshold is now closer to zero
cards.explanation: The gap between rest and threshold widens from 15 mV to 25 mV, so more excitatory input must sum at the trigger zone before an impulse is produced. Being closer to zero is not the same as being easier to reach; what matters is the distance from the resting potential. Threshold sets the firing decision directly, so it certainly affects rate. The resting potential of -70 mV is still well below -45 mV, so spontaneous firing would not occur.

cards.q: A neuron fires steady trains of action potentials even when every synapse onto it is blocked. Which change best explains this?
cards.a: Its resting potential has drifted up to threshold at the trigger zone.
options: Its cell body has stopped synthesizing membrane proteins
Its dendrites have lost the ability to generate graded potentials
Its axon terminal is releasing transmitter without Ca2+ entry
Its resting potential has drifted up to threshold at the trigger zone
cards.explanation: With no synaptic drive, the only way the trigger zone can keep reaching threshold is for the membrane potential itself to sit at or above threshold, which happens when the resting potential becomes less negative. Losing dendritic graded potentials would reduce firing, not cause it. Runaway release at the terminal would affect the next cell downstream and could not generate impulses at the trigger zone. Halting protein synthesis in the soma degrades the neuron over days rather than driving it to fire.

cards.q: Which glial cell forms the myelin sheath around axons in the brain and spinal cord?
cards.a: The oligodendrocyte.
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
The microglial cell
cards.explanation: Oligodendrocytes wrap central axons, sending out several arms so that one cell myelinates segments on many different axons. Astrocytes support synapses and the blood brain barrier but make no myelin. Schwann cells do make myelin, but only in the peripheral nervous system. Microglia are the immune cells of the CNS and remove debris rather than insulate axons.

cards.q: Which glial cell myelinates axons in peripheral nerves?
cards.a: The Schwann cell.
options: The satellite cell
The oligodendrocyte
The Schwann cell
The ependymal cell
cards.explanation: Schwann cells wrap peripheral axons, one cell per internode, and the same cell type also ensheathes unmyelinated peripheral fibers. Satellite cells are the other peripheral glia, but they surround cell bodies in ganglia rather than axons. Oligodendrocytes do the equivalent job in the CNS only. Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal and have no role in myelination.

cards.q: Which glial cell lines the ventricles of the brain and helps produce and circulate cerebrospinal fluid?
cards.a: The ependymal cell.
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
cards.explanation: Ependymal cells form the epithelium lining the ventricles and central canal, and their cilia keep cerebrospinal fluid moving while specialized ependymal cells of the choroid plexus secrete it. Astrocytes touch capillaries and help regulate what enters the brain, but they do not secrete cerebrospinal fluid. Microglia are phagocytes. Oligodendrocytes are the myelinating cells of the CNS.

cards.q: Which cell serves as the resident phagocyte and immune defender of the central nervous system?
cards.a: The microglial cell.
options: The astrocyte
The satellite cell
The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
cards.explanation: Microglia patrol the CNS, engulf pathogens and dead cells, and prune damaged synapses, which makes them the immune arm of nervous tissue. Astrocytes react to injury by forming a scar, but they are not phagocytes. Satellite cells support neuron cell bodies in peripheral ganglia. Ependymal cells line fluid spaces and have no defensive role.

cards.q: Which glial cell takes up excess K+ from the extracellular fluid around active neurons?
cards.a: The astrocyte.
options: The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The Schwann cell
The oligodendrocyte
cards.explanation: Astrocytes soak up the K+ that leaks out during repeated action potentials and spread it through their network, which keeps extracellular K+ near 4 mEq/L and keeps neurons from drifting toward threshold. Oligodendrocytes insulate axons and take no part in ion buffering. Microglia respond to damage. Schwann cells are peripheral and support single axons rather than managing the ionic environment of the brain.

cards.q: Which cells surround and support neuron cell bodies inside peripheral ganglia?
cards.a: Satellite cells.
options: Microglia
Astrocytes
Ependymal cells
Satellite cells
cards.explanation: Satellite cells form a capsule around the somata in dorsal root and autonomic ganglia, regulating the chemical environment much as astrocytes do centrally. Astrocytes perform that role, but only inside the CNS. Ependymal cells are confined to the ventricles and central canal. Microglia are also CNS residents and are phagocytic rather than supportive.

cards.q: Which glial cell is the most abundant in the central nervous system?
cards.a: The astrocyte.
options: The microglial cell
The ependymal cell
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
cards.explanation: Astrocytes are the most numerous glia in the brain and spinal cord, which fits the breadth of their jobs: potassium buffering, transmitter clearance, metabolic support and induction of the blood brain barrier. Microglia are a small fraction of the total. Ependymal cells are limited to the lining of fluid spaces. Schwann cells are numerous but are peripheral cells and are not found in the CNS at all.

cards.q: Which glial cell clears glutamate from the synaptic cleft after excitatory transmission?
cards.a: The astrocyte.
options: The astrocyte
The microglial cell
The oligodendrocyte
The ependymal cell
cards.explanation: Astrocyte processes wrap synapses and carry transporters that pull glutamate out of the cleft, ending the signal and protecting neurons from overexcitation. Microglia sample the environment for damage but do not perform transmitter reuptake. Oligodendrocytes contact axons rather than synapses. Ependymal cells line the ventricles, far from most synapses.

cards.q: How does the relationship between a myelinating cell and the axons it serves differ between the CNS and the PNS?
cards.a: One oligodendrocyte myelinates segments on several axons, while one Schwann cell myelinates one segment of one axon.
options: One Schwann cell serves many axons, while an oligodendrocyte serves one
One oligodendrocyte serves several axons, one Schwann cell serves one
Both cell types wrap exactly one internode on exactly one axon
Both cell types wrap the entire length of a single axon by themselves
cards.explanation: An oligodendrocyte extends multiple processes and myelinates an internode on each of several nearby central axons, while a Schwann cell wraps its whole body around a single internode of a single peripheral axon. Giving the Schwann cell the many-axon job reverses the two cell types. Restricting both to one internode on one axon ignores the branching of oligodendrocytes. No glial cell myelinates a whole axon by itself, which is why nodes of Ranvier exist between successive cells.

cards.q: Astrocyte potassium uptake fails in a region of cortex during heavy neuronal activity. Predict what happens to the neurons there.
cards.a: Extracellular K+ rises, the neurons depolarize, and they become more excitable.
options: Nothing changes, because the Na+/K+ ATPase handles all K+ removal
Extracellular K+ falls, the neurons hyperpolarize and become silent
Extracellular Na+ rises, so action potentials become larger than normal
Extracellular K+ rises, the neurons depolarize and become more excitable
cards.explanation: Each action potential leaks K+ into a small extracellular space, and if astrocytes do not take it up, the K+ equilibrium potential moves toward zero and drags the resting potential closer to threshold. Falling K+ would hyperpolarize cells, which is the opposite of what unbuffered activity produces. Sodium influx during firing tends to lower extracellular Na+ slightly rather than raise it. The pump helps restore gradients but works too slowly on its own to hold extracellular K+ steady during bursts of firing.

cards.q: Bacteria reach the brain tissue of a patient. Which glial cell population responds first by multiplying and engulfing the invaders?
cards.a: Microglia.
options: Oligodendrocytes
Microglia
Satellite cells
Ependymal cells
cards.explanation: Microglia are derived from the same lineage as macrophages, and they proliferate and phagocytose when they detect pathogens or debris in nervous tissue. Oligodendrocytes are highly specialized for making myelin and cannot phagocytose. Ependymal cells line fluid spaces and provide no defense. Satellite cells exist only in peripheral ganglia, so they cannot respond to an infection in the brain.

cards.q: A narrow ependymal-lined channel between two ventricles becomes blocked while cerebrospinal fluid continues to be produced upstream. What is the immediate consequence?
cards.a: Fluid accumulates upstream and pressure inside the ventricle rises.
options: Production stops at once, so total fluid volume stays normal
Fluid accumulates upstream and pressure inside the ventricle rises
The blood brain barrier opens to let the extra fluid escape
Astrocytes take over fluid production to bypass the block
cards.explanation: Cerebrospinal fluid is secreted continuously, so if the outflow path is closed the fluid backs up behind the obstruction and stretches the ventricle. Secretion by choroid plexus does not shut off in response to a downstream block. The blood brain barrier controls solute movement between blood and brain and is not a drainage route. Astrocytes support the barrier but do not secrete cerebrospinal fluid.

cards.q: A drug blocks astrocyte glutamate transporters at excitatory synapses. Predict the effect on the postsynaptic neuron.
cards.a: Glutamate lingers in the cleft, so the neuron is excited longer than normal.
options: Glutamate lingers in the cleft, so excitation lasts longer than normal
Glutamate is never released, so the neuron receives no excitation at all
Glutamate is converted to an inhibitory transmitter in the cleft
The postsynaptic membrane becomes impermeable to Na+ and Ca2+
cards.explanation: Astrocyte uptake is the main way glutamate is removed, so blocking it leaves transmitter bound to receptors and prolongs the excitatory postsynaptic potential, an effect that can become damaging if it continues. Release from the presynaptic terminal is a separate process and is untouched. Nothing in the cleft converts glutamate into an inhibitory transmitter. Postsynaptic channel proteins are not blocked by a transporter inhibitor.

cards.q: Astrocyte end feet help induce tight junctions between brain capillary endothelial cells. What does this predict about which substances enter the brain easily?
cards.a: Small lipid-soluble molecules cross readily while water-soluble ones need transporters.
options: All molecules cross freely, since the junctions only slow blood flow
Only large proteins cross, because they are carried across in vesicles
Small lipid-soluble molecules cross while water-soluble ones need carriers
Water-soluble molecules cross freely and lipid-soluble ones are excluded
cards.explanation: Tight junctions close off the path between endothelial cells, so entry has to be through the cell membranes, which favors small lipid-soluble molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and many anesthetics. Free passage for everything is exactly what the barrier prevents. Large proteins are the least likely to cross, not the most. Saying water-soluble molecules pass freely reverses the chemistry, since it is lipid solubility, not water solubility, that lets a substance slip through a membrane.

cards.q: A peripheral nerve is crushed but the connective tissue sheath stays intact. Which glial cell makes regrowth of the severed axons possible?
cards.a: The Schwann cell.
options: The oligodendrocyte
The astrocyte
The Schwann cell
The ependymal cell
cards.explanation: Schwann cells survive the injury, clear debris with macrophages, and line up in columns that guide the regrowing axon back toward its target, which is why peripheral nerves can recover. Oligodendrocytes are central cells, and the molecules they leave behind actively inhibit regrowth. Astrocytes react to central injury by forming a dense scar that also blocks regeneration. Ependymal cells have no role in peripheral repair.

cards.q: An autoimmune attack targets a protein found only in oligodendrocyte myelin. Which pattern of deficits is predicted?
cards.a: Lesions in the brain, spinal cord and optic nerve, with peripheral nerves spared.
options: Weakness in the hands and feet only, with the brain entirely spared
Loss of cerebrospinal fluid production and enlarging ventricles
Loss of sensation in dorsal root ganglia with normal central conduction
Brain, spinal cord and optic nerve lesions with peripheral nerves spared
cards.explanation: Oligodendrocytes myelinate only central axons, and the optic nerve is a central tract despite its name, so an antibody against their myelin produces scattered central lesions while Schwann cell myelin in peripheral nerves is untouched. A pure hands and feet pattern points to peripheral myelin instead. Cerebrospinal fluid production depends on ependymal cells, which carry different proteins. Dorsal root ganglion cell bodies are supported by satellite cells, so they are not the target here.

cards.q: During a stroke, astrocytes near the damaged tissue lose ATP and can no longer run their glutamate transporters. Trace the consequence for nearby neurons.
cards.a: Glutamate builds up, drives excessive Ca2+ entry, and injures neurons beyond the original zone.
options: Glutamate is trapped inside astrocytes, so nearby synapses go silent
Glutamate builds up, drives excess Ca2+ entry, and injures nearby neurons
Neurons hyperpolarize and are protected from further damage
Myelin is stripped from nearby axons by the excess transmitter
cards.explanation: Glutamate uptake is an active process, so when ATP fails the transmitter accumulates, overstimulates receptors, and lets enough Ca2+ into neurons to trigger destructive enzymes, which is how injury spreads into tissue that was initially viable. Failing transporters leave glutamate outside the astrocyte rather than trapping it inside. Excess glutamate depolarizes rather than hyperpolarizes its targets. Demyelination is an immune or metabolic process affecting the myelinating cell, not a direct action of transmitter.

cards.q: The narrow passage draining one ventricle is obstructed by a tumor. Put the resulting events in the right order.
cards.a: Secretion continues, fluid accumulates upstream, the ventricle expands and presses on brain tissue.
options: The ventricle collapses, then secretion rises to refill the space
Secretion continues, fluid accumulates, the ventricle expands on brain tissue
Microglia secrete extra fluid to flush the obstruction away
Astrocytes absorb the extra fluid, so pressure never changes
cards.explanation: Choroid plexus secretion is not regulated by downstream pressure, so it continues, fluid piles up behind the block, and the expanding ventricle compresses the surrounding tissue. A ventricle upstream of a block fills rather than collapses. Microglia are phagocytes and secrete no fluid. Astrocytes buffer ions and support the barrier but cannot absorb a continuously produced fluid volume fast enough to prevent a rise in pressure.

cards.q: The same patient severs a nerve in the forearm and a tract in the spinal cord. The forearm recovers function over months while the cord deficit is permanent. Which glial difference best explains this?
cards.a: Schwann cells guide peripheral regrowth, while oligodendrocytes and astrocytes obstruct it centrally.
options: Schwann cells guide peripheral regrowth while central glia obstruct it
Central neurons lack cell bodies capable of protein synthesis after injury
Peripheral axons are shorter, so they need less axonal transport to regrow
Microglia remove peripheral debris but are absent from the spinal cord
cards.explanation: The peripheral environment is permissive because Schwann cells proliferate, form guiding columns, and release growth factors, while the central environment is hostile because oligodendrocyte myelin carries inhibitory molecules and reactive astrocytes build a glial scar. Peripheral axons are often the longer of the two, so length does not explain the difference. Central neurons retain full protein synthesis in the soma. Microglia are abundant in the spinal cord and clear debris there as well.

cards.q: What is a node of Ranvier?
cards.a: A short gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed.
options: A short gap in the myelin sheath where the axon membrane is exposed
The junction between an axon terminal and its target cell
The point where an axon branches into several collaterals
The layer of myelin laid down by a single glial cell
cards.explanation: Nodes are the bare patches between successive myelin segments, and they are where ions can actually cross the membrane. The junction with a target cell is a synapse, a different structure entirely. A branch point is a collateral and has nothing to do with myelin. The stretch of myelin made by one glial cell is the internode, which is the insulated region between two nodes.

cards.q: What is the name for the way an action potential travels along a myelinated axon?
cards.a: Saltatory conduction.
options: Continuous conduction
Electrotonic spread
Saltatory conduction
Antidromic conduction
cards.explanation: Saltatory comes from the Latin for jumping, and it describes the impulse being regenerated only at the nodes so that it appears to leap from node to node. Continuous conduction is the slower pattern seen in unmyelinated axons, where every patch of membrane must fire in sequence. Electrotonic spread is the passive, decremental flow of current, which is what happens under the myelin between nodes. Antidromic conduction means travel in the direction opposite the normal one.

cards.q: What does the myelin sheath do to the electrical properties of the axon membrane it covers?
cards.a: It raises membrane resistance and lowers membrane capacitance.
options: It lowers membrane resistance and raises membrane capacitance
It raises membrane resistance and lowers membrane capacitance
It raises both membrane resistance and membrane capacitance
It leaves both unchanged and simply protects the axon from injury
cards.explanation: Stacking many lipid layers around the axon makes it much harder for ions to leak out, which is high resistance, and separates the charges farther apart, which is low capacitance. Both changes push more of the local current forward inside the axon to the next node. Lowering resistance would do the opposite and let current escape. Myelin does provide some mechanical protection, but the reason it speeds conduction is electrical.

cards.q: Which axon conducts action potentials fastest?
cards.a: A large diameter myelinated axon.
options: A small diameter unmyelinated axon
A large diameter myelinated axon
A small diameter myelinated axon
A large diameter unmyelinated axon
cards.explanation: Diameter and myelination both raise conduction velocity, so the fastest fibers in the body have both, reaching about 100 m/s. Small unmyelinated fibers are the slowest, near 1 m/s, and they carry slow pain and temperature. Either factor alone helps: a large unmyelinated axon or a small myelinated one falls in between. The two effects work through the same principle, which is getting current farther down the axon before it leaks away.

cards.q: Where are voltage-gated Na+ channels concentrated along a myelinated axon?
cards.a: At the nodes of Ranvier.
options: Spread evenly along the entire axon under the myelin
At the nodes of Ranvier
In the myelin sheath itself, between the lipid layers
Only at the axon terminal, where transmitter is released
cards.explanation: Channels are clustered in the bare nodal membrane, which is the only place ions can cross, so that is where the impulse is regenerated. Spreading them evenly would waste them, since the membrane under the myelin cannot pass current across itself anyway. Myelin is made of stacked glial membrane and holds no functional axonal Na+ channels. The terminal has voltage-gated Ca2+ channels for release, but Na+ channels are needed all along the axon to keep the impulse alive.

cards.q: What is myelin mostly made of?
cards.a: Lipid, in many wrapped layers of glial cell membrane.
options: Lipid, in many wrapped layers of glial cell membrane
Collagen fibers secreted into the space around the axon
Extracellular fluid trapped between connective tissue sheets
Dense cytoskeletal protein extending out of the axon
cards.explanation: Myelin is glial plasma membrane wrapped repeatedly around the axon, and because membrane is largely lipid the sheath is an excellent electrical insulator. Collagen surrounds nerves in the connective tissue sheaths but is not myelin. Trapped fluid would conduct current rather than block it, defeating the purpose. Cytoskeletal protein such as neurofilament fills the inside of the axon rather than forming the sheath.

cards.q: Roughly how fast does a large myelinated axon conduct compared with a small unmyelinated one?
cards.a: About 100 m/s versus about 1 m/s.
options: About 10 m/s versus about 9 m/s
About 100 m/s versus about 1 m/s
About 1 m/s versus about 100 m/s
About 1000 m/s versus about 100 m/s
cards.explanation: The fastest human fibers run near 100 m/s and the slowest unmyelinated C fibers near 1 m/s, roughly a hundredfold spread, which is why touch reaches awareness well before slow burning pain. A difference of only 10 percent would not produce that everyday experience. Pairing 1 m/s with the myelinated fiber reverses the two, giving the insulated axon the slower speed. Nothing in the body conducts at 1000 m/s; that is far beyond what any axon achieves.

cards.q: Besides myelination, which axon property most affects conduction velocity?
cards.a: Axon diameter.
options: The length of the axon
The number of dendrites on the cell body
The amount of transmitter stored in the terminal
Axon diameter
cards.explanation: A wider axon offers less internal resistance to the flow of current along its core, so depolarization spreads farther and faster ahead of the impulse. Axon length changes how long the trip takes but not the speed of travel. Dendrite number affects how much input the cell integrates, not how fast its output moves. Stored transmitter matters at the synapse after the impulse has already arrived.

cards.q: Myelin is stripped from a stretch of axon while the nodes keep their Na+ channels. Predict what happens to conduction through that stretch.
cards.a: Current leaks out across the bare internode, so the next node may not reach threshold.
options: Conduction speeds up, because current no longer has to cross the sheath
Current leaks across the bare internode and the next node may not fire
Conduction is unchanged, since the nodes still have their channels
The axon fires continuously, because the membrane is now unprotected
cards.explanation: Myelin keeps local current inside the axon so it arrives at the next node still strong enough to open Na+ channels there; without it, current escapes across the exposed membrane and the depolarization arriving downstream may fall below threshold, slowing conduction or blocking it. Removing insulation cannot speed conduction, since the whole advantage came from the insulation. Intact nodal channels are not enough if too little current reaches them. Bare membrane between nodes has few voltage-gated channels, so spontaneous firing is not the expected result.

cards.q: A demyelinating disease affects the largest myelinated sensory fibers first. Which sensation is most likely to be lost earliest?
cards.a: Vibration and position sense.
options: Slow burning pain
Itch from the skin surface
Warm temperature sensation
Vibration and position sense
cards.explanation: Vibration and proprioception travel on the largest, most heavily myelinated afferents, so they are the first modalities to fail when myelin is the target. Slow burning pain runs on unmyelinated C fibers, which have no myelin to lose and are therefore spared early. Warm temperature also travels on unmyelinated fibers. Itch is likewise carried by small unmyelinated afferents, so it persists while position sense fades.

cards.q: Two axons have the same diameter, but one is myelinated and one is not. What accounts for the myelinated axon conducting faster?
cards.a: It regenerates the impulse only at nodes instead of at every patch of membrane.
options: It regenerates the impulse only at nodes rather than at every patch
It has a larger resting potential, so it starts closer to threshold
It has more Na+/K+ ATPase pumps to restore its gradients faster
It carries a larger action potential, which travels farther per step
cards.explanation: Opening channels takes time, so an axon that must fire every square micrometer of membrane in sequence is slow, while one that can skip the insulated internodes and fire only at nodes covers the same distance in far fewer steps. Pump density affects long-term gradient maintenance, not the speed of a single impulse. Resting potential is about the same in both axons and is not what myelin changes. Action potential amplitude is set by the ion gradients and is essentially the same in both.

cards.q: A person with partial demyelination notices that symptoms worsen when body temperature rises, for example in a hot bath. What does this suggest about the affected axons?
cards.a: They are conducting at the edge of failure, so a small change tips them into block.
options: Heat destroys myelin directly, so the damage is permanent each time
They have lost all their nodal Na+ channels and cannot conduct at all
They are conducting at the edge of failure, so a small change blocks them
Heat increases transmitter release, which fatigues the muscles
cards.explanation: Where myelin is thinned, each node barely receives enough current to reach threshold, so anything that shortens the time channels stay open, as warming does, can push conduction from marginal to blocked, and symptoms return until the temperature falls. Complete loss of nodal channels would produce a fixed deficit rather than one that comes and goes. A hot bath does not strip myelin, which is why the change is reversible. The problem is conduction along the axon, not transmitter release at the synapse.

cards.q: A signal must travel 1 m from the toe to the spinal cord. How long does it take on a fiber conducting at 50 m/s compared with one conducting at 1 m/s?
cards.a: About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms.
options: About 50 ms versus about 100 ms
About 2 ms versus about 100 ms
About 20 ms versus about 50 ms
About 20 ms versus about 1000 ms
cards.explanation: Time equals distance divided by velocity, so 1 m at 50 m/s takes 1/50 of a second, which is 20 ms, and 1 m at 1 m/s takes a full second, or 1000 ms. That fiftyfold gap is why a sharp prick registers almost instantly while the aching pain behind it arrives about a second later. The values of 50 ms, 2 ms and 100 ms come from dividing in the wrong direction or from mixing seconds with milliseconds.

cards.q: Imagine an axon whose myelin is normal but whose internodes are made much shorter, so nodes occur far more often. What happens to conduction velocity?
cards.a: It falls, because the impulse must be regenerated more times over the same distance.
options: It rises, because more nodes mean more Na+ channels overall
It is unchanged, since only myelin thickness matters
It falls, because the impulse is regenerated more times per meter
It falls to zero, because current cannot cross a short internode
cards.explanation: Each regeneration costs the time it takes Na+ channels to open, so packing in extra nodes adds delays without adding distance covered per step. More channels do not help if the limiting factor is how many times you must stop and rebuild the signal. Internode length matters alongside sheath thickness, so the property is not fixed by thickness alone. Conduction still succeeds; a short internode passes current easily, it is just an unnecessary stop.

cards.q: A patient has patchy demyelination in the optic nerve. Vision is dim and blurred rather than absent, and a recording shows the visual response arriving late but still present. What explains this pattern?
cards.a: Conduction is slowed and partly blocked, so a smaller and less synchronized signal arrives late.
options: Conduction is slowed and partly blocked, so a late, scattered signal arrives
The photoreceptors have been destroyed, so no signal is generated
The optic nerve axons are cut, so no signal can reach the brain at all
The brain is ignoring the signal, though conduction is entirely normal
cards.explanation: Patchy demyelination leaves some fibers conducting slowly, some blocked, and the surviving impulses arriving at scattered times, which produces a delayed and weakened response rather than an absent one. Destroyed photoreceptors would abolish the signal at its source, and no delayed response would be recorded. Cut axons would likewise give no response. A normal-conduction explanation cannot account for a measured delay.

cards.q: A nerve conduction study shows greatly slowed velocity with response amplitude close to normal. What does this point to?
cards.a: Demyelination with the axons themselves largely intact.
options: Loss of many axons with the remaining ones normally myelinated
Failure of transmitter release at the neuromuscular junction
A muscle disease with normal nerve function throughout
Demyelination with the axons themselves largely intact
cards.explanation: Velocity depends on the insulation and the geometry of the fibers, while amplitude depends on how many axons are firing, so slow but full-sized responses say the wiring is intact and the insulation is not. Losing axons would drop the amplitude while leaving the surviving fast fibers at close to normal speed, the opposite pattern. A junction problem shows up as a fading response with repeated stimulation rather than slowed conduction. Muscle disease would not slow a nerve at all.

cards.q: An immune attack strips myelin from motor axons in the peripheral nerves of the legs over a few days. Predict the combination of findings.
cards.a: Weakness with reduced or absent reflexes, while slow pain sensation is preserved.
options: Loss of slow pain first, with strength and reflexes preserved
Weakness with exaggerated reflexes, because the muscles are irritable
Weakness with reduced reflexes, while slow pain sensation is preserved
No weakness, because unmyelinated motor fibers take over the work
cards.explanation: Motor axons to skeletal muscle are large and heavily myelinated, so stripping myelin blocks or delays their impulses and both voluntary strength and the reflex response fall away, while unmyelinated C fibers carrying slow pain keep working. Reflexes depend on those same large fibers, so they weaken rather than increase. Slow pain rides on fibers with no myelin to lose, so it is not the first casualty. There are no unmyelinated motor fibers to skeletal muscle that could substitute.

cards.q: A motor axon 1 m long normally conducts at 50 m/s. Demyelination drops its velocity to 5 m/s. How much extra delay does a command now take to reach the muscle, and what is the functional result?
cards.a: About 180 ms of extra delay, so movements become slow and poorly timed.
options: About 180 ms extra, so movements become slow and poorly timed
About 20 ms extra, too small to change anything the person notices
About 2 s extra, so voluntary movement becomes impossible
No extra delay, because the impulse amplitude is unchanged
cards.explanation: One meter at 50 m/s takes 20 ms and at 5 m/s takes 200 ms, so the difference is 180 ms, a delay long enough to disrupt the timing that smooth movement and balance depend on. The 20 ms figure is the normal transit time rather than the added delay. Two seconds would require a velocity near 0.5 m/s, well below what this axon still manages. Conduction time depends on velocity, not amplitude, so unchanged amplitude does not protect the timing.

cards.q: Which motor protein carries cargo down the axon away from the cell body?
cards.a: Kinesin.
options: Dynein
Kinesin
Myosin
Tubulin
cards.explanation: Kinesin walks toward the plus end of a microtubule, which in an axon points away from the soma, so kinesin is the anterograde motor. Dynein walks the other way and handles retrograde traffic. Myosin is a motor too, but it moves along actin filaments and drives muscle contraction and short-range movements. Tubulin is not a motor at all; it is the subunit that polymerizes into the microtubule track.

cards.q: Which motor protein carries cargo back up the axon toward the cell body?
cards.a: Dynein.
options: Kinesin
Dynein
Actin
Myosin
cards.explanation: Dynein moves toward the minus end of a microtubule, which in an axon points back toward the soma, making it the retrograde motor. Kinesin is its anterograde counterpart. Actin is a filament protein, not a motor, and it forms the track that myosin uses. Myosin does not carry cargo the length of an axon, since actin filaments do not run continuously along it.

cards.q: Which cytoskeletal element serves as the track for fast axonal transport?
cards.a: Microtubules.
options: Neurofilaments
Actin microfilaments
Microtubules
Collagen fibrils
cards.explanation: Microtubules run lengthwise through the axon with a consistent orientation, which gives the motor proteins both a road and a sense of direction. Actin microfilaments are concentrated just under the membrane and in the terminal, where they support short-range movement. Neurofilaments provide structural support and set axon caliber, and they are themselves cargo of slow transport rather than a track. Collagen is an extracellular protein and is not inside the axon at all.

cards.q: What does fast anterograde transport carry to the axon terminal?
cards.a: Membrane-bound organelles such as synaptic vesicles and mitochondria.
options: Worn out organelles being returned for breakdown
Neurofilaments and other structural proteins of the cytoskeleton
Membrane-bound organelles such as vesicles and mitochondria
Free ribosomes that will synthesize protein in the terminal
cards.explanation: Fast anterograde transport moves membrane-enclosed cargo, so vesicles carrying transmitter enzymes, membrane proteins and mitochondria all travel this way at a few hundred millimeters per day. Worn organelles travel the other direction, back to the soma, by retrograde transport. Cytoskeletal proteins move by slow transport, which is a hundred times slower. Axon terminals contain almost no ribosomes, which is precisely why protein has to be shipped from the cell body.

cards.q: What does fast retrograde transport carry back to the cell body?
cards.a: Used organelles and growth factor signals taken up at the terminal.
options: Used organelles and growth factor signals picked up at the terminal
Newly made synaptic vesicles ready to be filled with transmitter
Fresh mitochondria heading toward the energy demands of the synapse
Soluble enzymes needed for transmitter synthesis in the terminal
cards.explanation: Retrograde traffic returns worn organelles for recycling and delivers signals such as nerve growth factor that the terminal has taken up, telling the soma the target has been reached. Newly made vesicles are anterograde cargo, since they are built in the cell body. Mitochondria travel both ways, but fresh ones heading to the synapse are moving anterograde. Enzymes for transmitter synthesis are also delivered outward, not returned.

cards.q: What does slow axonal transport carry, and at roughly what rate?
cards.a: Cytoskeletal proteins and soluble enzymes, at about 1 mm per day.
options: Synaptic vesicles and transmitter enzymes, at about 400 mm per day
Cytoskeletal proteins and soluble enzymes, at about 1 mm per day
Membrane receptors in vesicles, at about 50 mm per hour
Mitochondria and membrane proteins, at about 100 mm per day
cards.explanation: Slow transport moves the axon's structural material, the neurofilaments, tubulin and cytosolic enzymes, at a rate measured in a millimeter or so per day, and it is anterograde only. Synaptic vesicles are fast anterograde cargo, moving hundreds of millimeters per day. Mitochondria are also fast cargo. Membrane receptors travel inside vesicles and therefore also use the fast system.

cards.q: A virus is taken up at a nerve terminal in the skin and later appears in the neuron cell body in the spinal cord. Which transport process moved it?
cards.a: Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein.
options: Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin
Slow transport, driven by cytoskeletal assembly
Simple diffusion along the length of the axon
Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein
cards.explanation: Movement from the terminal back to the soma is retrograde by definition, and dynein is the motor that walks in that direction, which is how viruses such as rabies and toxins such as tetanus reach the central nervous system. Anterograde transport would carry the virus the wrong way, out toward the terminal. Slow transport is anterograde only and far too slow. Diffusion over a distance of a meter would take years and is not a viable route.

cards.q: A virus lying dormant in a dorsal root ganglion cell body reactivates and produces a rash in the skin served by that neuron. Which transport process delivered it?
cards.a: Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin.
options: Fast retrograde transport, driven by dynein
Fast anterograde transport, driven by kinesin
Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins
Transport through the bloodstream to the skin
cards.explanation: Moving from the cell body out to the peripheral ending is anterograde, and kinesin is the motor for that direction, which is why the rash appears in exactly the skin field served by that one ganglion. Retrograde transport is the route the virus took originally, on its way in from the skin. Slow transport carries structural proteins and would take far too long for a rash that develops over days. A bloodborne route would scatter the rash rather than confining it to one sensory territory.

cards.q: A drug depolymerizes microtubules inside an axon. Predict the effect on axonal transport.
cards.a: Both fast anterograde and fast retrograde transport fail.
options: Only anterograde transport fails, since dynein uses actin instead
Only retrograde transport fails, since kinesin does not need a track
Transport speeds up, because cargo is no longer tethered to a track
Both fast anterograde and fast retrograde transport fail
cards.explanation: Kinesin and dynein both walk on microtubules, differing only in which end they head toward, so destroying the track stops traffic in both directions and the terminal is cut off from the cell body. Dynein does not use actin; that is myosin. Kinesin cannot move cargo without a track any more than dynein can. Removing the track leaves cargo stranded rather than free to travel faster.

cards.q: A severed peripheral axon regrows at roughly 1 mm per day. Which transport process sets that pace?
cards.a: Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins.
options: Fast anterograde transport of synaptic vesicles
Diffusion of ions into the growing tip
Fast retrograde transport of growth factor signals
Slow transport of cytoskeletal proteins
cards.explanation: A regrowing axon has to build new cytoskeleton along its whole new length, and tubulin and neurofilaments arrive only by slow transport at about a millimeter per day, which matches the observed regeneration rate almost exactly. Fast anterograde transport runs hundreds of times faster and is not the bottleneck. Retrograde signals report back to the soma but do not supply building material. Ion movement is not what limits the construction of a new axon segment.

cards.q: A motor neuron axon is 1000 mm long and fast anterograde transport runs at 400 mm per day. About how long does a newly made vesicle take to reach the terminal?
cards.a: About 2.5 days.
options: About 2.5 hours
About 25 days
About 2.5 days
About 400 days
cards.explanation: Dividing 1000 mm by 400 mm per day gives 2.5 days, a reminder that even the fast system takes real time over the length of a limb. Getting hours instead of days means the rate was read as millimeters per hour. Twenty-five days would follow from a rate of 40 mm per day, ten times too slow. Four hundred days confuses the rate with the answer.

cards.q: A mutation disables dynein in a group of motor neurons. Predict what happens to the neuron over time.
cards.a: New material still reaches the terminal, but debris and survival signals no longer return, and the cell degenerates.
options: New material still reaches the terminal, but nothing returns, and the cell fails
Nothing changes, because kinesin can carry cargo in either direction
The terminal is starved of vesicles at once, so transmission stops within hours
The axon regrows faster, because retrograde traffic no longer blocks the track
cards.explanation: Kinesin is intact, so outward delivery continues, but the neuron loses the return line that clears worn organelles and carries trophic signals such as nerve growth factor back to the nucleus, and without that feedback the cell slowly degenerates. Immediate loss of transmission would require the anterograde motor to fail. Kinesin is directional and cannot substitute for dynein. Removing traffic in one direction does not accelerate growth, since growth depends on outward supply and on the trophic signals that are now lost.

cards.q: In one experiment kinesin is blocked, and in another dynein is blocked, both at the midpoint of a long axon. Where does cargo pile up in each case?
cards.a: Kinesin block piles cargo on the cell body side; dynein block piles it on the terminal side.
options: Kinesin block piles cargo on the soma side, dynein block on the terminal side
Both blocks pile cargo on the terminal side of the axon
Both blocks pile cargo on the cell body side of the axon
Kinesin block piles cargo on the terminal side, dynein block on the soma side
cards.explanation: Cargo accumulates behind the stalled motor, and anterograde cargo approaches the block from the soma side while retrograde cargo approaches it from the terminal side, so the swelling appears on opposite sides in the two experiments. Having both pile up in the same place would require both motors to travel in the same direction. Putting the kinesin pile on the terminal side reverses the directions the two motors travel.

cards.q: An axon 500 mm long is cut near the cell body. Fast anterograde transport runs at 400 mm per day and slow transport at 1 mm per day. Compare the two delivery times and explain what this predicts about recovery.
cards.a: Fast cargo would need about a day and slow cargo about 500 days, so rebuilding the axon takes many months.
options: Fast cargo takes about a day, slow cargo about 500 days, so recovery takes months
Both take about a day, so recovery should be complete within a week
Fast cargo takes 500 days and slow cargo about a day, so recovery is quick
Neither matters, because a cut axon is rebuilt from the terminal inward
cards.explanation: Dividing 500 mm by each rate gives about 1.25 days for the fast system and 500 days for the slow system, and since the new axon must be built from cytoskeletal proteins carried by slow transport, that slower figure is what governs the timeline, which is why nerve recovery is measured in months. Equal times would require the two systems to run at the same rate, and they differ by several hundredfold. Giving the fast system the 500 day figure swaps the two rates. Regrowth proceeds outward from the surviving stump, supplied by the cell body, not inward from a terminal that is no longer connected.
